parts.title: Why Tip Screens Often Ask for More Than You Planned
parts.part1:
At checkout, an awkward moment may arrive before payment is finished. The screen offers a few tip rates, with one number shown first. That number can change the question in your mind—from “What did I plan to give?” to “Which option should I choose?”

A peer-reviewed study published in 2014 examined more than 13 million credit-card taxi transactions in New York City. Around a $15 fare, the tip menu changed suddenly. At fares just below and just above that price, passengers saw different default tip menus.

Passengers who saw the higher suggested rates left more money. In this taxi setting, the screen itself changed the final tip. The first number became a starting point for the decision.
parts.part2:
But there was a limit. When the suggested rate was too high, some customers did not choose a smaller custom amount. They left no credit-card tip at all.

A 2022 policy brief describes high suggested tips as a business choice. It says they can increase store revenue, while having little measurable effect on customer satisfaction or return visits. That offers one reason a screen may show a number higher than a customer’s first plan.

Today, digital payment screens can sometimes suggest tips as high as 35 percent. The small box at the end of a meal is no longer just recording a decision. It is helping shape the decision before it is made.
parts.point_one_heading: The old tip jar worked differently
parts.point_one_body: A 2022 policy brief places today’s screen in a longer change. In the US, restaurant tipping rose from about 10 to 15 percent in the early 1970s to about 20 percent by the late 1990s. The report argues that digital screens also create “guilt tipping.” The choice feels less private when a worker is nearby and can see it.
parts.point_two_body: A 2026 US survey found signs of fatigue. Seventy-eight percent called tipping ridiculous, and 44 percent said they had reduced their tips. The share who felt they had to tip on a screen fell from 66 percent in September 2025 to 59 percent in 2026. Thirty-six percent chose a custom amount. These are self-reported answers, not proof of cause.
parts.in_one_line: The tip screen starts the conversation with a number, but it does not control the final answer. A stronger suggestion may bring in more money from some customers—and bring a zero from others.

parts.title: When the Tip Screen Starts the Negotiation
parts.part1:
At the end of a taxi ride or a meal, the payment screen asks one small question:

“How much would you like to tip?”

But the screen usually gives an answer first.

It shows a few suggested percentages. The first choices may be higher than the amount you planned to give. That first number can change the whole decision.

A 2014 study looked at more than 13 million credit card taxi payments in New York City.

The researchers found a useful natural test. For fares just below $15 and just above $15, the suggested tip menu changed suddenly. The rides were almost the same price, but some passengers saw a different menu.
parts.part2:
Passengers who saw higher suggested rates left more money.

This suggests that the number on the screen can become a starting point. People may begin with that number instead of their own first idea.

But there was a catch.

When the suggested tip was too high, some customers did not simply choose a smaller amount. They chose zero.

So a high default can raise the tip from some customers. But it can also push other customers away from tipping by card completely.
parts.point_one_heading: The screen makes a private choice public
parts.point_one_body:
In the United States, restaurant tipping rose from about 10 to 15 percent in the early 1970s to about 20 percent in the late 1990s, according to one policy brief.

Digital payment screens can now show tips as high as 35 percent. One expert argues that this changes the feeling of the moment. With a cash tip jar, the choice could be more private. With a screen held by an employee, the customer may feel watched. He calls this pressure “guilt tipping.”
parts.point_two_heading: Customers are starting to push back
parts.point_two_body:
A 2026 survey found that 78 percent of respondents said tipping had become unreasonable. Forty-four percent said they were tipping less than the year before.

Among consumers prompted by a digital screen to tip, the share who felt they had to leave a tip fell from 66 percent in September 2025 to 59 percent in 2026. And 36 percent said they chose a custom amount instead of a suggested rate.

These are survey answers, not proof that the screen caused the change. But they suggest that many customers are increasingly pushing back against digital prompts to tip.
parts.in_one_line: A tip screen offers the first answer before you make your own choice. A higher number may bring in more money, but if it feels too high, some customers may choose nothing.
